strengths: The paper proposes a useful combination of density-ratio-based optimization and graph-based semi-supervised learning. The inductive prediction rule allows the approach to accommodate both sampled unlabeled points and predefined candidate pools.

The reported empirical results are promising, particularly on the synthetic functions and NATS-Bench. Comparisons include BORE and LFBO with several classifier families and GP-based optimization, with 20 repeated runs and standard errors.

The appendices investigate kernel parameters, unlabeled sample counts, sampling distributions, pool subsampling, and threshold ratios. These studies help expose practical sensitivities and acknowledge that unlabeled data does not consistently improve performance.
weaknesses: The central benefit of unlabeled data is insufficiently isolated. The no-transduction comparison in Figure 12 uses a fixed kernel parameter of 0.5, whereas the main experiments learn this parameter and frequently obtain much larger values. The no-transduction method also performs better in some ablation settings. A comparably tuned kernel-only baseline under the main experimental protocol, together with a control for the randomized tie-breaking heuristic, is needed to distinguish improvements from semi-supervision, kernel selection, and acquisition optimization.

The proposed exploration mechanism remains inadequately supported. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated points does not ensure Assumption 4.1: high-density regions can connect points with opposite threshold labels. Expanding the region assigned high positive-class probability also does not establish better exploration or global optimization. Appendix C explicitly acknowledges that the cited independent-sampling theory does not apply to this sequential setting, leaving the stronger explanatory claims without a supporting argument or direct quantitative evaluation.

Although the baseline set is substantial, it lacks random search and a matched exploration-enhanced BORE/LFBO control. These are especially relevant because excessive exploitation is the stated problem, and related work addressing it is acknowledged. The runtime study only compares the proposed method across subset sizes, so its computational tradeoff against competitors remains unclear.

Evidence for broader applicability is limited. All continuous synthetic benchmarks are two-dimensional. The 64-dimensional MNIST experiment uses a representation trained on 440,000 labeled triplets to predict the same digit values subsequently optimized. This supplies substantial target-specific information; comparison against directly ranking candidates with the pretrained classifier would clarify what the optimization stage contributes.

Important implementation details remain unspecified, including input scaling, kernel-parameter optimization settings, propagation hyperparameters, and how continuous L-BFGS-B optimization produces valid candidates from arbitrary finite pools. These omissions impede reproduction, particularly without accompanying code. There is also a correctable inconsistency in Section 4.1: the entrywise definition of P is column-normalized, whereas P = D^{-1}W is row-normalized; the convention used in Equation 7 and the experiments should be clarified.
